overview: Herrerasaurus was one of the largest predators of the Ischigualasto fauna, reaching six metres long around 231 million years ago. Its flexible intramandibular joint — a sliding articulation between the dentary and postdentary bones unique among early dinosaurs — allowed a powerful grip on struggling prey.

Its phylogenetic position remains debated: most analyses treat it as either a basal saurischian (Herrerasauridae) or an early theropod. Either way it documents the very rapid ecological diversification of early dinosaurs in the Late Triassic of South America.

articles.title: Discovery and systematic controversy
articles.body: Reig named the species in 1963 from fragments; a near-complete skeleton found in 1988 by Sereno and Novas transformed understanding. The intramandibular joint is its most distinctive anatomical feature. Whether Herrerasaurus sits within Theropoda or as a more basal saurischian is one of the most actively debated questions in early dinosaur phylogenetics.

articles.title: Anatomy
articles.body: Despite its size, Herrerasaurus retained five digits on the hand (two vestigial) and relatively short arms. The pelvis already shows the perforate acetabulum diagnostic of all dinosaurs. Powerful hindlimbs confirm full bipedality from the outset of its existence.

articles.title: Triassic context
articles.body: At 231 Ma, dinosaurs were not yet dominant: rhynchosaurs, cynodonts and rauisuchians (such as Saurosuchus) were more abundant. Herrerasaurus was the apex dinosaurian predator in an ecosystem still dominated by non-dinosaurian archosaurs, making it a key taxon for understanding predator-prey dynamics at the origin of the dinosaur radiation.

record.description: Herrerasaurus ischigualastensis was an early predatory dinosaur from the Ischigualasto Formation of Argentina. Multiple skeletons, including complete skulls and very substantial postcrania, document a lightly built biped; whether herrerasaurids lie inside Theropoda or just outside the sauropodomorph-theropod split remains debated.
facts: Ischisaurus cattoi and Frenguellisaurus ischigualastensis are generally regarded as synonyms of Herrerasaurus.
Recurved serrated teeth and grasping hands support carnivory.
Its mixture of primitive and derived features makes root-level classification unstable.

animalParagraphs: Herrerasaurus was a medium-sized biped, three to six metres long, that lived in the Ischigualasto valley of north-west Argentina about 230 million years ago, when dinosaurs were still a minor part of the fauna. It shared its habitat with large rhynchosaurs and cynodonts and with the crocodile-line predator Saurosuchus.

Its skull was long and narrow with a sliding joint in the lower jaw, and its teeth were recurved and serrated. The hands had three long clawed fingers plus two reduced ones and were clearly built for grasping. The hindlimbs were long and the pelvis carried features found in later theropods, though in an early combination.

Named in 1963 by Osvaldo Reig from a partial skeleton, Herrerasaurus was transformed in 1988 when Paul Sereno's team found a skeleton with a complete skull. That specimen made it, for a time, the best-known early dinosaur, and it remains central to debates about what the first dinosaurs looked like.
animalHighlights: A complete skull and several substantial skeletons make it one of the best-documented Triassic dinosaurs.
Recurved, serrated teeth and grasping hands document a predatory lifestyle.
Its mix of ancestral and theropod-like features keeps its place on the dinosaur tree unsettled.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Serrated, recurved teeth, a flexible lower jaw and grasping hands indicate carnivory. Prey is inferred from the fauna rather than from gut contents.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Long hindlimbs and short forelimbs in articulated skeletons show two-legged walking and running; speed is estimated from proportions only.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: The most complete skeleton is around four metres; larger individuals are known from partial remains, so the upper figure is an extrapolation.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Proportions come from articulated skeletons; skin, colour and any feather-like covering are not preserved.

presentation.classificationSummary: Herrerasaurus gives its name to Herrerasauridae, a group of early predatory dinosaurs that includes Staurikosaurus and Gnathovorax. Analyses disagree on whether herrerasaurids are the earliest branch of Theropoda or sit outside the theropod–sauropodomorph split as basal saurischians.

related.reason: A smaller contemporary from the same formation, once thought to be a theropod.
A Brazilian herrerasaurid known from a single partial skeleton.
An unambiguous early theropod from Ischigualasto for comparison.

questions.title: Theropod or not?
questions.copy: Herrerasaurids combine ancestral hips with theropod-like hands and skulls. Whether they are early theropods or fall outside Theropoda altogether changes with each new analysis.

questions.title: How big did it get?
questions.copy: The complete skull belongs to a roughly four-metre animal. Larger partial specimens once named Frenguellisaurus suggest six metres, but no complete large individual exists.

questions.title: What did the earliest dinosaurs look like?
questions.copy: Herrerasaurus is often used as a model, but its specialised predatory features may not reflect the dinosaur ancestor.

panel.headline: Several skeletons and a complete skull from the Ischigualasto badlands.
panel.standfirst: Herrerasaurus is known from the 1963 holotype postcranium, a 1988 skeleton with an essentially complete skull, and additional partial skeletons including material once named Ischisaurus and Frenguellisaurus. Together they cover the whole skeleton.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is represented, most by more than one individual, including a complete skull and articulated limbs, pelvis and tail.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: A complete skull with lower jaws and teeth, cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal vertebrae, both girdles, forelimbs with complete hands, and hindlimbs with feet, spread across the holotype, PVSJ 407 and referred specimens.
knownRemains.note: No single specimen preserves everything, so composite reconstructions combine individuals of somewhat different sizes.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: A complete skull with braincase and lower jaws in PVSJ 407, plus partial skulls and maxillae in other specimens.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series, with ribs and chevrons, in the holotype and referred skeletons.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Complete pelvis and scapulocoracoid, forelimbs with five-fingered grasping hands, and hindlimbs with feet.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: None. No skin, feathers, gut contents or eggs are known.
